scope: Trusts and foundations run by office-holders and party officers (Rajiv Gandhi Foundation/Charitable Trust/Institute for Contemporary Studies and the Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust on the Congress side; Vivekananda International Foundation, India Foundation, Prajna Pravah and Overseas Friends of BJP-USA on the BJP/RSS side), and foreign money to parties (the 2014 Delhi High Court finding that Vedanta subsidiaries' donations to BOTH BJP and Congress breached FCRA 1976, and the 2016/2018 retrospective Finance Act amendments that legalised this back to 1976). claims.innocentReading: Corporate groups routinely use holding, logistics or finance subsidiaries for ordinary business reasons; a subsidiary purchasing bonds is not itself evidence of round-tripping or foreign control absent proof that the ultimate parent's foreign shareholding crosses the post-2016 statutory threshold.

claims.killIf: The subsidiary is shown to be wholly Indian-owned at every tier

narratives.claim: The Rajiv Gandhi Foundation took Chinese Communist Party money in 2005-06, in effect paid for by the same government the family led, to produce research favourable to Beijing.
narratives.strongestCase: RGF's own FY2005-06 annual report lists the Chinese embassy as a donor/partner organisation (documented, political-trusts:c008); RGF's promoted think tank RGICS produced a study around that time favourable to an India-China free trade agreement (per Indian Express's account of the BJP's allegation); the government's 2022 cancellation order itself cites a ₹1.35 crore Chinese-embassy receipt as a ground (fcra-actions:c057 in the sibling file, tier alleged there).
narratives.strongestCounter: A donor being listed in an annual report is routine institutional disclosure, not evidence of quid pro quo; RGF was never shown in the sources we found to have altered any government position because of the donation; Congress's response reframed the story as a distraction from unresolved India-China border tensions and BJP/RSS's own historical CPC contacts; the amount, source and even the precise statutory provision breached were disputed or unstated across the record we assembled.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The actual FCRA cancellation order or committee report (not yet public in any source we reached) specifying the statutory provision breached and the exact sum; RGF's own FC-4 returns for FY2005-06 and FY2006-07, if published.

narratives.claim: India Foundation is an opaquely-funded, RSS/BJP-aligned think tank whose governing council doubles as a shadow cabinet, and the Doval family runs an undisclosed offshore financial network connected to it.
narratives.strongestCase: The Wire's 2017 reporting (as paraphrased by Wikipedia) that four 2014-vintage Union ministers, including Nirmala Sitharaman, remained India Foundation directors after taking office is a genuine, documented institutional-overlap fact (political-trusts:c015); its conferences were reportedly sponsored by international firms (Boeing, DBS Bank) even as its leadership said no foreign funding was received — those two statements are in some tension, though sponsorship of a conference and a foreign 'contribution' are legally distinct under FCRA. The Caravan's 2019 report on a Cayman-Islands-linked hedge fund run by Ajit Doval's other son, Vivek, is a separate claim about a family member's business, not about India Foundation's own accounts.
narratives.strongestCounter: The 'offshore network' claim is about a private individual's (Vivek Doval's) business, not an institution, and is exactly the kind of family-as-actor claim this project's rules say not to encode as fact; the claim was contested enough that Vivek Doval sued for defamation, and in Dec 2020 Jairam Ramesh apologised in court 'for any hurt the statements may have caused' — though an apology in a defamation suit is not the same as a finding that the underlying facts were false, and could equally reflect a litigation-cost calculation.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: India Foundation's own audited accounts (not located); the full text of the Caravan report and any follow-up reporting on the defamation suit's actual disposition, neither of which we could render in this session (JS-rendered sites).

narratives.claim: The 2016 and 2018 Finance Act amendments to the FCRA were a bipartisan cover-up: Parliament, controlled by the BJP but with the tacit acquiescence of a Congress unwilling to reopen its own exposure, retrospectively legalised donations both major parties had received unlawfully.
narratives.strongestCase: The underlying predicate fact is documented, not alleged: the Delhi High Court in 2014 found, on largely undisputed facts, that both BJP and Congress received donations from Sterlite/Sesa (majority-owned by UK-incorporated Vedanta Resources plc) that met FCRA 1976's definition of a foreign-source contribution (political-trusts:c018-c021, primary judgment text). The retrospective legalisation via two money bills (2016 and 2018), reaching back to 1976, is corroborated by at least one further secondary source (Wikipedia's Electoral Bond Scheme article) beyond general public knowledge, and — tellingly — was NOT contested as to substance by either party at the time, which is itself informative given both had an equal interest in the outcome.
narratives.strongestCounter: We could not, in this session, open the bare statutory text or a neutral legislative-tracker (PRS) confirming the precise section numbers and the exact 1976 retrospective date, so some of the legal specifics rest on a single secondary characterization rather than primary confirmation; it is also possible to read the amendment as a legitimate, prospectively-reasoned narrowing of an over-broad 1976-era 'foreign source' test (many wholly-domestically-controlled Indian companies with passive foreign shareholders above 50% would otherwise be permanently unable to donate) rather than as bad-faith retrospective immunity — the amendment's critics and defenders dispute the characterization, not the underlying legislative fact.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The Finance Act 2016 and 2018 bare texts (indiacode.nic.in was unreachable this session); a PRS Legislative Research bill-track summary for either Finance Bill (prsindia.org 404'd under every slug tried); confirmation of whether the ADR petition against the retrospective amendment was disposed of, withdrawn, or remains pending before the Supreme Court (not established in sources we reached).

symmetryCheck: Applying the same lens (documented FCRA enforcement action, or a documented foreign-money controversy, tied to a national party's central leadership or its aligned think tanks) produced a strikingly asymmetric result in what we could actually find and verify this session — but the asymmetry is partly an artifact of press coverage and partly an artifact of this session's access limits, and one important sub-question is symmetric on the primary evidence we DID verify. On the Congress side: RGF and RGCT were both investigated from 2020 and had their FCRA registrations cancelled in Oct 2022 on stated grounds including a Chinese-embassy donation and a Zakir Naik/IRF donation (detailed in this directory's fcra-actions.json); RGICS and the Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust were named in the same 2020 probe. On the BJP/RSS side, applying the identical search — did VIF, India Foundation, Prajna Pravah or OFBJP-USA face any documented FCRA cancellation, suspension or comparable enforcement action — found NOTHING in any source we could open this session (see voids). That zero could mean these organisations are in fact compliant and never triggered scrutiny, or it could mean our access to the Indian press archive was badly degraded this session (see gaps: most major outlets' search functions returned 403s, JS-only shells, or unrelated fallback content for every guessed URL) — we cannot distinguish these two explanations from what we found, and it would be wrong to present the zero as proof of a double standard. Where we DID verify a genuinely symmetric documented fact — the 2014 Delhi High Court's finding that BOTH BJP and Congress received unlawful foreign-source donations via Vedanta subsidiaries, and the subsequent 2016/2018 retrospective amendments reported to have legalised this for both parties identically — the record is symmetric on its face: same violation, same two respondents, same legislative fix applied to both. That is the one part of this file's brief we can say, with real confidence, treated both parties identically.

gaps: Could not verify OFBJP-USA's reported August-2020 US FARA registration (this file's brief specifically asked for it): efile.fara.gov timed out on every attempt (both direct GET and via WebFetch); fara.report's connection was rejected by proxy policy ('connect_rejected'); no press source describing the filing was successfully opened.

Could not open the bare text of Finance Act 2016 or Finance Act 2018 (indiacode.nic.in connections timed out repeatedly) or a PRS Legislative Research bill-track page for either Finance Bill (every URL slug we tried 404'd, unlike the FCRA Amendment Bill 2020 page, which loaded correctly) — the 2016/2018 retrospective-amendment claims in this file are tiered 'reported', resting on a single secondary source (Wikipedia's Electoral Bond Scheme article), not 'documented'.

Could not establish whether the Association for Democratic Reforms' Supreme Court appeal against the retrospective FCRA amendment (referenced in the task brief as 'the SC appeal withdrawn') was withdrawn, disposed of, or remains pending — no primary or press source confirming this was opened this session.

Could not verify any FCRA-registered personal/family trust of Naveen Patnaik, Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy or M.K. Stalin (sansad.in is an Angular SPA not reachable via curl; Wikipedia's search API was rate-limited fleet-wide for most of the session).

This session's WebSearch tool was exhausted (fleet-wide 200/200 budget) before this file's research began; all research here relied on WebFetch and curl through the proxy. Separately, WebFetch-via-Bing was unreliable for this file's compound queries: it repeatedly returned generic dictionary/entity results (e.g., a query containing 'Rajiv Gandhi Foundation' returned only generic Rajiv Gandhi biography links; a query containing 'Vedanta' returned only Vedanta-philosophy results) regardless of the rest of the query string, across roughly a dozen attempts — this appears to be a tool-level degradation specific to Bing SERPs fetched this way, not a proxy block, and is worth flagging for other agents in this fleet.

Several major Indian outlets (livemint.com, hindustantimes.com's search, indiatoday.in, thehindu.com, business-standard.com's search, theprint.in, scroll.in's search, thewire.in's search) either 403'd, JS-rendered with no static content, or returned unrelated fallback articles for guessed URLs in this environment; where a real article was reachable via curl (indianexpress.com, hindustantimes.com direct article URLs, thehindu.com/thewire.in/caravanmagazine.in for title-confirmation only) it is cited; where not, the gap is recorded rather than the claim being asserted.
